newsitem.title: FRANCE: French capital markets closing report.
newsitem.headline: French capital markets closing report.

text.p: French bond futures tumbled for the fourth successive session as a slide in the mark against the dollar fanned concerns the German central bank could raise short-term rates to support its currency.

Traders said the near-term outlook for the September bond future was fragile both on a technical and fundamental basis with concerns about supply and German jobs figures on Wednesday likely to add to the currency headache.
The close at 129.20 was seen as bearish for the contract and few had any clear notion where support would kick in if dollar strength knocked the price below 129, a level not seen since June 25.

An analyst at a French brokerage said comments from Bundesbank economist Otmar Issing and Germany's Ifo institute on Tuesday had exacerbated the impact of the dollar strength on European bond and interest rate futures.
"The foreign exchange markets will continue to be a source of tension after Issing. It could prompt traders to try and put the Bundesbank to the test," he said.
Ifo said the Bundesbank could raise rates if the dollar/mark parity reached 1.90 and Issing said the weakening of the mark was "certainly gives us something to think about".
One mitigating factor for the French bond market could be support from domestic investors. Traders said domestic investors were seen buying bonds at the lows on Tuesday.

The French Treasury said it would be selling 21-23 billion francs of long-dated OATs and 300-500 million Ecu of 10-year OATs on Thursday and while analysts said there could be some covering just before the sale it probably wouldn't weigh to heavily on prices.

French interest rate futures suffered along with German interest rate futures after the decline in the mark as low as 1.8832 against the dollar but some analysts said the PIBOR selloff looked overdone.
"I'm puzzled as to why people automatically assume the Bank of France will have to increase if the Bundesbank does," Sonja Gibbs, bond analyst at Nomura International said.

The view that france won't necessarily follow may be behind the current weakness in mark/Paris," she said. "It's absolutely defensible on all possible economic and political grounds - maybe they would slavishly follow the Bundesbank but I just don't think they have to."
The French franc slipped as low as 3.3788 against the mark from 3.3713 late on Monday, its lowest level since July 21.
It touched a low of 6.3555 against the dollar, down 22.5 percent so far in 1997.
